meta.title: The Note That Makes It Minor
meta.summary: Of the three notes that drop from A major to A minor, only the third — the b3 — decides whether a chord is minor; the b6 and b7 colour a key without it.

spans.text: Three notes dropped going from A major to A minor, and they are not equal partners. Drop only the third and everything already sounds minor. Drop only the sixth, on its own, and it doesn't — the chord underneath hasn't moved at all.
Here's why, in terms you already have from the CAGED pathway: a chord is a root, a third and a fifth. The root names the chord. The fifth is identical in both —
E
above an A root, major or minor, doesn't move. That leaves the third as the only note free to carry the difference:
A C# E
against
A C E

. It isn't a metaphor. It's an accounting — two notes are pinned down, and only one is left to do anything at all. The root has to stay the root or the chord has a different name entirely; the fifth barely varies chord to chord in the first place. That leaves the third holding the entire question of major versus minor by itself.
That gives you the minor triad:
. Hold onto that shorthand — a later chapter puts it into five windows across the neck.
The third is the note to listen for. It's the only one of the three that lives inside the chord itself, not just the scale around it.
The
b6
and
b7
are colour, not identity. They live in the scale, not in the triad, and a piece that only ever touches
is already minor without either of them. Take them away and the chord doesn't stop being minor; take away the
b3
instead and it does, no matter how much of the surrounding scale you leave in place.

So what do major and minor actually name? Two chords on the same root, with the third sitting three semitones up instead of four. Said plainly and without overclaiming: the acoustic difference is real — a minor triad is slightly rougher and less fused than a major triad on the same root, and its root reads as a touch less clearly defined. What that difference
means

is a separate question. The familiar claim that minor sounds sad is mostly something a listener learns from the music around them, not something the notes themselves contain, and this pathway isn't going to hand it to you as settled fact.
The rougher, less settled sound of a minor triad against a major one is measurable. What a listener decides that roughness means is learned, and it isn't the same lesson.
Two places to put an ear on this.
Ear Trainer
drills the interval itself — major third against minor third, isolated from everything else.
Chord Detector
listens to what you actually played and tells you whether it came out minor.

Knowing which note makes a chord minor is only half the story, though. It doesn't explain why seven notes that never change — the ones this chapter opened with — can sound like they belong to two different keys, C major one moment and A minor the next, with nothing in the note list to tell them apart.
